source_text: 7.1. Atque ipsi penitus perspicitis vos ipsos, si quando de rebus disceptatis obscuris et naturalia pergitis reserare secreta, et ipsa quae dicitis, quae adseveratis, quae capitali plerumque contentione defenditis, nescire vos et unumquemque suspiciones suas < pro > probatis et comprehensis pertinaci obluctatione tutari. 2. Quid enim, si verum perspiciam, etiamsi omnia saecula in rerum investigatione ponantur, scire per nos possumus, quos ita caecos et superbos nescio quae res protulit et concinnavit invidia, ut, cum nihil sciamus omnino, fallamus nos tamen et in opinionem scientiae sub inflati pectoris tumore tollamur? 3. Ut enim divina praeteream et naturali obscuritate res mersas, potest quisquam explicare mortalium, id quod Socrates ille conprehendere nequit in Phaedro [Pl. Phaedr. 230], homo quid sit aut unde sit, anceps varius mobilis pellax multiplex multiformis, 4. in quos usus prolatus sit, cuius sit excogitatus ingenio, quid in mundo faciat, cur malorum tanta experiatur examina, 5. utrum ne illum tellus uliginis alicuius conversa putore tamquam vermes animaverit, tamquam mures, an fietoris alicuius et fabricatoris manu liniamenta haec eorporis atque oris acceperit formam? 6. Potest, inquam, scire in medio haec posita atque in sensibus constituta communibus, quibus causis mergamur in somnos, quibus evigilemus, quibus modis fiant insomnia, quibus visa: 7. immo quod ambigit in Theaeteto Plato [Plat. Theaet. 158 b], vigilemus aliquando an ipsum vigilare quod dicitur somni sit perpetui portio, et quod agere videamur, insomnium; 8. cum videre nos dicimus, radiorum et luminis intentione videamus an rerum imagines advolent et nostris in pupulis sidant; utrum sapor in rebus sit an palati contagionibus fiat quibus ex causis pili nigrorem ingenitum ponant neque omnes pariter sed paulatim adiciendo canescant; 9. quid sit quod humores universi unum corpus efficiant mixtione, solum oleum respuat immersionem in se pati, sed in suam naturam impenetrabile semper perspicue colligatur; 10. ipse denique animus, qui inmortalis a vobis et deus esse narratur, cur in aegris aeger sit, in infantibus stolidus, in senectute defessus delira effutiat et insana? 11. Quorum infirmitas et inscientia miserabilis hoc magis est, ut cum fieri possit ut veri aliquid aliquando dicamus, et hoc ipsum nobis incertum sit, an veri aliquid dixerimus.
pass_a_gloss: On obscure natural questions you yourselves see you do not know what you fiercely defend—each guarding suspicions as if proved. Blind pride inflates a reputation of knowledge; even common matters (sleep, dreams, sight, taste, soul) escape certainty, so that if we ever say something true we cannot be sure we did.
pass_b_english: 7.1. And you yourselves thoroughly see yourselves, whenever you dispute about obscure matters and proceed to unlock natural secrets, that you do not know even those things which you say, which you assert, which you commonly defend with capital contention, and that each one guards his own suspicions with stubborn wrestling as if they were proved and grasped. 2. For what, if I look at the truth, even if all ages were spent in investigating things, can we know through ourselves—we whom I know not what thing has brought forth so blind and proud, and envy has put together, so that, though we know nothing at all, we still deceive ourselves and are lifted into an opinion of knowledge under the swelling of an inflated breast? 3. For to pass over divine things and things sunk in natural obscurity, can any of mortals explain—that which Socrates in the Phaedrus cannot grasp—what a human is or whence he is, two-sided, varying, movable, deceitful, manifold, many-formed, 4. for what uses he was brought forth, by whose ingenuity he was devised, what he does in the world, why he experiences such swarms of evils, 5. whether the earth, turned by the rottenness of some moisture, animated him like worms, like mice, or whether he received these outlines of body and the form of the face by the hand of some potter and craftsman? 6. Can he know, I say, these things placed in the midst and set in common senses: by what causes we sink into sleeps, by what we wake, by what means dreams happen, by what visions: 7. indeed what Plato doubts in the Theaetetus—whether we ever wake or that which is called waking is a portion of perpetual sleep, and what we seem to do is a dream; 8. when we say we see, whether we see by an aiming of rays and light or whether images of things fly and settle in our pupils; whether taste is in things or happens by contacts of the palate; by what causes hairs lay aside inborn blackness and not all equally but by gradual adding grow white; 9. what it is that makes all liquids one body by mixture, while oil alone refuses to suffer immersion into itself, but is always clearly gathered into its own nature impenetrable; 10. finally the mind itself, which is said by you to be immortal and a god, why in the sick it is sick, in infants dull, in old age worn out it pours out delirious and insane things? 11. Whose weakness and pitiable ignorance is this the more, that although it can happen that we sometimes say something true, even this itself is uncertain for us—whether we have said something true.

lemmas.sense: you do not know what you assert

choices.choose: Pagan natural disputes rest on guarded suspicions, not secured knowledge
reject: You possess certain science of obscure natures

choices.choose: Pride’s fake knowledge cannot certify truth even about everyday senses and the soul
reject: Human cleverness settles sleep, sight, and soul with certainty
